claims.text: Integrating high-dimensional compositional descriptors with phonon-dispersion calculations will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than current approaches.
Intrinsic chemical disorder in high-entropy alloys enhances phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering from chemical disorder reduces phonon thermal conductivity.
Conventional arc melting followed by homogenization heat treatment produces a near-single-phase, chemically disordered high-entropy-alloy microstructure.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder produces mass and strain-field fluctuations that influence phonon scattering.
Combinatorial atomic arrangements in high-entropy alloys scatter heat-carrying phonons.
Combined compositional descriptors and phonon-dispersion curves can capture the effect of chemical disorder on phonon lifetimes.
Accounting for disorder-induced changes in phonon lifetimes will improve predictions of phonon thermal conductivity.
The proposed approach will have significantly lower prediction errors than heuristic or simpler machine-learning methods.
Predictions from the proposed approach will align more closely with experimental thermal-conductivity measurements.
Traditional models based mainly on empirical trends and simplified descriptor sets often miss the role of phonon scattering in chemically disordered systems.
The proposed approach is primarily applicable to multi-principal-element alloys that retain a single-phase disordered structure.
Significant phase segregation or atomic ordering may limit the approach's applicability.
Dominant electronic contributions to thermal transport may limit the approach's applicability.
Training-data gaps and the complexity of phonon-disorder interactions make the magnitude of the expected accuracy improvement uncertain.
